messages.subject: Re: Marine mammal distance sampling survey -
parts:
Here is the summary of advice from Eric Rexstad in response to my earlier=
post:

1: I think your 2km systematic offset surveyed a couple of times during =
the season is probably fine. Better than random selection because being =
systematic ensures even coverage throughout the study area.
2: Once you have transitted through your study area on your 12 transects=

, your ship needs to get back to port. Could you not return along your "=
offset" transects?

3: There is no necessity for your transects to run the full 40km width o=
f your study area. You could use "segmented transects" using the term us=
ed in the Distance survey design engine. It has the disadvantage of havi=

ng "off-effort" in your study area.

--

messages.subject: Re: Marine mammal distance sampling survey -
parts:
Dear Elaine,

Something else that also comes to mind here is that if you are sampling=20
the entirety of the sampling area you need to be careful. This is an=20
issue that tends to be ignored and that was alluded to by

Cassey, P. & Mcardle, B. An assessment of distance sampling techniques=20
for estimating animal abundance Environmetrics, 1999, 10, 261-278

which refer in their abstract that

"If the proportion of the study area surveyed by transects is large=20
however, then the presence of large between PSU variation will cause the=20
variance estimates from program DISTANCE to be a sizeable overestimate."

If I recall correctly there is also something on this on the=20
introduction to distance sampling 2001 book, but I don't have my copy=20
with me.

The issue is that the conventional estimation of the encounter rate=20
available in Distance assumes that one uses a "small" number of=20
transects of the available sampling units (in theory, there would be an=20
infinite number of sampling units). In the limit, if you sample the=20
entire area of inference, there is no encounter rate variance, the only=20
variance that exists is from the detection probability (assuming no=20
individuals, not clusters). However, if you input the data into Distance=20
ignoring this, the software assumes these were a random sample of=20
transects and assumes that the variance is valid. It's like comparing=20
variance estimates in a finite population in which (1) you account or=20
(2) you don't account for the fact that the population is finite. If the=20
population is finite, and you sample a large proportion of the available=20
sampling units, you can massively overestimate variance if you ignore=20
the finite population correction factor.

The above is only considering spatial variability, and assuming a single=20
sampling event. If you have also temporal variability to care for (i.e.=20
you have a sample of days over a year, but you want inferences about the=20
average density over that year) then things can become less clear,=20
because given that animals can go in and out of your study area during=20
the period of interest, then even covering the entire area you still=20
have (temporal) variability associated with your data. You need to think=20
carefully what is the variability you are interested in (spatial,=20
temporal or both).

Given how you described your study area, I wonder if this is worth=20
considering. I hope this has not made it more confusing than you'd hope f=
or.

cheers,

Tiago
